title: Alternative Views: Zetrix AI’s meltdown — the missed red flags
text:
Alternative Views: Zetrix AI’s meltdown — the missed red flags Monday 16 Nov 2026 BURSA SGX Home 
 Edge Weekly Make The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google This article first appeared in Forum, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 16, 2026 - November 22, 2026 
 In less than three months, Zetrix AI Bhd (KL: ZETRIX ) — once hailed as a front runner in Malaysia’s push towards a digital economy — has effectively turned to ashes. Today, the company is fighting to stay afloat under a debt load exceeding RM3.4 billion.
 The red flags around Zetrix AI’s trajectory were visible, particularly in the last three years, yet investors and bankers failed to pay heed to them. Now, thousands of retail and institutional shareholders are staring at massive equity losses while financial institutions holding the company’s bonds have begun to book steep write-offs.
 Among them, a non-bank-backed fund house, AmanahRaya Investment Management Sdn Bhd, has already written off its exposure to Zetrix AI’s sukuk.
 Looking back at the rapid unravelling of the former stock market darling that rode the government’s push to provide online payment services beginning in 2010, several key takeaways stand out from Zetrix AI’s meltdown.
 The first lies in the composition of Zetrix AI’s board, which appeared ill-equipped to oversee a high-spending technology enterprise, alongside an over-reliance on its key executive, group managing director Wong Thean Soon, better known as T S Wong.
 For a company positioning itself at the cutting edge of blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) solutions, it is a glaring anomaly that virtually none of its directors were from the information technology sector.
 Apart from the 56-year-old Wong, the board consisted largely of retired civil servants, former senior police officers and corporate executives. Two of its longest-serving directors — a former politician and an ex-policeman — had sat on the board for two decades.
 This raises an uncomfortable question: did the board truly understand the technical realities and commercial risks behind Zetrix AI’s multi-billion-ringgit spending spree on blockchain and AI development?
 A board’s fundamental duty is to temper the animal spirits of ambitious founders who may overleverage a company in pursuit of aggressive expansion. Directors must act as risk-averse restraints even when doing so triggers discomfort or boardroom friction.
 Four of Zetrix AI’s seven directors resigned last month, a move that was too little, too late. The financial damage had already been done, and the board had failed in its duty to sound the alarm much earlier.
 The second lesson is the importance of understanding a company’s core business and having a clear sense of the underlying value of its assets before committing capital to it.
 Zetrix AI’s traditional cash cow — its near-monopoly on online payment and renewal services for the Road Transport Department (JPJ) and the Immigration Department — began to face structural threats following the 2018 change in the federal government. By 2023, both government agencies had rolled out their own competing digital applications.
 In response, Zetrix AI pivoted aggressively after 2020 towards blockchain infrastructure and AI. It entered into joint ventures with Mimos Bhd to build commercial applications around the MyDigital ID ecosystem and teamed up with HeiTech Padu Bhd (KL: HTPADU ) to pursue large-scale e-government IT projects — a partnership that has since lapsed.
 To fuel this pivot, Zetrix AI poured more than RM1.5 billion into developing AI solutions, channelling substantial capital into Chinese technology firms for personal AI development. Combined, spending on blockchain and AI swelled to account for more than 50% of the company’s total assets as at Dec 31, 2025.
 Yet few outside the company truly understood what products were being built, who the paying customers were, or how those intangible assets could be reliably valued.
 In its 2025 credit assessment, MARC Ratings Bhd noted that Zetrix AI’s blockchain platform had recorded 5.2 million transactions across more than 750,000 accounts. Following Zetrix AI’s default on a RM25 million sukuk obligation last week, MARC stopped its rating coverage.
 With hindsight, did the Zetrix AI technology platform genuinely have 750,000 active paying accounts or were the rating agency and investment analysts simply relying on management’s representations?
 While Zetrix AI undeniably possesses technological assets, commercialising them to service billions in debt requires fresh capital and Wong’s stewardship. With funding dried up and Wong’s personal stake whittled down to a fraction following forced selling, the recoverable value of those assets remains deeply uncertain.
 The third takeaway is a classic reminder not to take headline earnings at face value.
 On paper, Zetrix AI did not look like a distressed company. Net profit was growing steadily, dividends were declared regularly and operating cash flow remained healthy.
 However, a close look at the cash flow statement reveals a widening structural gap. Since the financial year ended Dec 31, 2021 (FY2021), Zetrix AI’s net cash outflow from investing activities consistently outpaced its operating cash flow. While the legacy business generated steady cash, it was nowhere near enough to fund the massive capital expenditure required for its blockchain and AI ambitions.
 That shortfall was plugged with debt.
 Up until FY2020, the company, then known as MY E.G. Services Bhd, was in a net cash position. From 2021 onwards, borrowings escalated rapidly, swelling to RM3.4 billion against cash reserves of RM541.2 million by mid-2026.
 The final lesson revolves around the personal financial health of a company’s main driver.
 In Zetrix AI’s case, the bulk of Wong’s shareholdings was pledged as collateral, leaving him heavily exposed whenever market sentiment turned. Meanwhile, unusually high daily trading volumes on Bursa Malaysia had long sparked market chatter of share “warehousing” arrangements.
 At the corporate level, Zetrix AI had also turned to share placements to raise cash, diluting existing shareholdings.
 It is noteworthy that in February this year, the International Finance Corporation — the private-sector investment arm of the World Bank — had subscribed to nearly 200 million new Zetrix AI shares at 78 sen apiece, betting that its digital public infrastructure and AI tools could be exported to other developing nations.
 The warning signs seen at Zetrix AI were similar to those in past Malaysian corporate implosions, most notably that of Serba Dinamik Bhd.
 Once an institutional darling in the oil and gas (O&G) sector, Serba Dinamik spiralled into one of Malaysia’s biggest corporate scandals after external auditors flagged discrepancies in its books — a saga that ended without any jail time for its top executives.
 Similarly, Zetrix AI was a market high-flyer until late August this year, when the forced selling of Wong’s shares triggered a cascading collapse, leaving stockbrokers, investment banks and retail investors nursing heavy losses.
 Time and again, seemingly credible companies fall apart due to unchecked, debt-fuelled expansion — resulting in lasting scars on market confidence.
 Just as banks remain wary of lending to the domestic O&G sector years after the failures of Serba Dinamik and SapuraKencana Bhd (now Vantris Energy Bhd under new ownership), Zetrix AI’s collapse will cast a long shadow.
 It may be a long time before another Malaysian blockchain or AI company secures institutional backing with the same ease.
